steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Multi-Objective Scheduling of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Workflows in Cloud Computing
summary: This technique replaces ad-hoc or single-objective execution strategies for deploying LLM-based multi-agent workflows onto heterogeneous cloud resources. It requires formulating workload scheduling as a multi-objective optimization problem and selecting among genetic or heuristic solvers, which introduces algorithmic complexity and a dependency on accurate latency and cost models of the underlying infrastructure. The approach can fail if the workload characteristics deviate from the modeled assumptions or if the chosen Pareto-optimal solution does not align with actual production priorities for latency, cost, or utilization.
rationale: The method addresses cloud resource orchestration at a scale and with infrastructure heterogeneity assumptions that exceed the reader's constrained single-GPU or API-based setup, requiring unavailable distributed infrastructure for implementation.
technique: Multi-Objective Scheduling of LLM Multi-Agent Workflows (MO-SAIC)
